o: Count substrings of s in which some character occurs at least k times. For 'abacb', k=2 the four valid substrings are listed in the statement; for 'abcde', k=1 every substring qualifies. Complement counting is easiest: total substrings minus those where every character appears fewer than k times. Badness is hereditary (substrings of bad substrings are bad), so a two-pointer window counts bad substrings in O(n).
k: Complement: answer = n(n+1)/2 - (#windows where max frequency < k), and the latter is countable with a sliding window since badness is monotone.

a.n: Approach 1: Brute Force with Frequency Counts
a.i: Enumerate all O(n^2) substrings, maintaining a frequency array as the right endpoint grows, and check whether any character reaches k. With n ≤ 3000 this is ~9M operations with an O(26) check — acceptable but wasteful.
s: For each left index, reset counts and extend right.
Track the running max frequency incrementally.
a.t: O(n^2) — all substring endpoints enumerated with O(1) incremental updates.

a.i: Count 'bad' windows (every character < k occurrences) with two pointers: for each right endpoint, shrink from the left while some character has reached k; afterwards left is the first start that makes the window good, so exactly left bad substrings end at r. Subtract from the total n(n+1)/2.
s: For each r, increment cnt of s[r].
While max(cnt) >= k, decrement cnt[s[left]] and advance left.
Accumulate left as the count of bad substrings ending at r; answer = n(n+1)/2 - bad.
a.t: O(26n) — each character enters and leaves the window once; the max scan is a constant 26.

w: Prefer the complement sliding-window solution; it generalizes to much larger n. Pitfalls: counting good windows directly with two pointers is awkward because goodness is not monotone under shrinking — always flip to the hereditary property. Watch 64-bit totals (up to ~4.5e9 substrings). Follow-up: count substrings where exactly one specified character reaches k, or the hard version with n up to 1e5 (same technique).
